title: Design a Scalable URL Shortener (TinyURL)
description: High-availability URL shortening service capable of handling 500M new links per month with a 100:1 read-to-write ratio and < 20ms p99 redirect latency.
hldPoints: High Throughput & Low Latency SLA: Engineered for peak QPS with sub-50ms p99 latency target and elastic horizontal auto-scaling.
Stateless Compute Fleet: Microservice pods for UrlShortenerService deployed across multiple Availability Zones behind L7 Application Load Balancers.
Distributed In-Memory Caching: Multi-tier Redis Cluster caching hot read paths (ShortUrl) using cache-aside / write-through with LRU eviction.
Database Partitioning & Sharding: Sharded relational/NoSQL storage partitioned by consistent hash of entity ID, with primary-replica async replication.
Resilience & Fault Tolerance: Multi-AZ active-active deployment, circuit breaker fast-fail mechanisms, and dead-letter queue (DLQ) event handling.
systemDesignDiagram:
flowchart TD
  Client([Client Browser / App]) -->|HTTPS REST / gRPC| LB[Application Load Balancer]
  LB --> ServiceFleet[UrlShortenerService Service Fleet]
  ServiceFleet -->|1. Check Cache| Cache[(Redis Cache Layer)]
  ServiceFleet -->|2. Query / Persist| DB[(Primary Database Cluster)]
  ServiceFleet -->|3. Event Stream| MessageQueue[(Kafka Message Log)]
  DB --> ReadReplicas[(Read Replicas)]
  MessageQueue --> WorkerFleet[Background Worker Fleet]
hldExplanation: The high-level architecture for Design a Scalable URL Shortener (TinyURL) is designed for global scale, zero single point of failure (SPOF), and high availability. Requests enter through Anycast DNS and edge CDN caching before hitting L7 Application Load Balancers. The stateless UrlShortenerService fleet inspects in-memory Redis caches before hitting partitioned database replicas, ensuring predictable low latency under high concurrency.
lldPoints: Strict SOLID Architecture: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) isolating domain models (ShortUrl) from service orchestration (UrlShortenerService).
Gang of Four Design Patterns: Implemented Strategy Pattern for swappable business algorithms, Factory Method for instantiation, and Observer for lifecycle events.
Thread-Safety & Synchronization: Constructed with atomic primitives, ReentrantLock, and ConcurrentHashMap for safe multi-threaded concurrency.
Extensible Domain Model: Clean interface contracts enabling polymorphic extensions without modifying tested production code.

relatedAnswers.question: How do you handle high-concurrency contention when millions of users interact with ShortUrl simultaneously?
relatedAnswers.interviewerIntent: Assessing candidate's deep knowledge of locking primitives, distributed concurrency, and database bottleneck prevention.
relatedAnswers.modelAnswer: To prevent write contention on ShortUrl, we combine distributed caching with optimistic concurrency control (OCC). For reads, requests hit distributed Redis clusters with 99%+ cache hit rates. For writes, we utilize Redis Lua scripts or atomic CAS operations, with version-based optimistic locking at the database layer (UPDATE ShortUrl SET status = :status, version = version + 1 WHERE id = :id AND version = :version). If high contention creates write hot-spots, we introduce queue buffering with Kafka partition keys to serialize updates per entity ID.
keyPoints: Optimistic locking using monotonically increasing version fields
Redis distributed locks with fencing tokens for cross-node coordination
Kafka topic partitioning by entity ID to serialize hot writes
Circuit breakers to fast-fail traffic during downstream latency spikes
relatedAnswers.tradeOffs: Pessimistic locking guarantees strict serializability but limits throughput and introduces deadlock risks. Optimistic locking maximizes throughput under moderate contention but requires client retry strategies during collisions.
relatedAnswers.edgeCases: Clock drift between servers when using timestamps instead of monotonic version numbers; network partitions causing split-brain master elections.

relatedAnswers.question: What is your data partitioning and sharding strategy for Design a Scalable URL Shortener (TinyURL) as data grows beyond single-node limits?
relatedAnswers.interviewerIntent: Evaluating horizontal scaling competence, sharding key selection, and avoidance of hotspot partitions.
relatedAnswers.modelAnswer: We employ consistent hashing across database shards using MurmurHash3 on the entity ID. This ensures uniform data distribution across nodes. We configure virtual nodes (e.g. 256 vnodes per physical node) to avoid partition skew. For cross-entity queries, we maintain secondary global indexes asynchronously updated via Change Data Capture (CDC) pipelines like Debezium into Elasticsearch.
keyPoints: Consistent hashing ring with 256 virtual nodes per physical machine
MurmurHash3 / CityHash for uniform 64-bit key distribution
Asynchronous CDC secondary indexing via Debezium and Elasticsearch
Zero-downtime shard rebalancing with dual-write migration protocols
relatedAnswers.tradeOffs: Hash sharding provides uniform distribution but makes range queries expensive (requiring scatter-gather across all shards). Range-based sharding supports efficient range scans but creates hot shards on recent data.
relatedAnswers.edgeCases: Celebrity entities / hot keys overwhelming a single shard; handling network partitions during shard migration.

tradeOffs: Consistency vs Availability (CAP Theorem): Choosing AP for high availability with eventual consistency vs CP for strict serializability.
Cache-Aside vs Write-Through: Cache-aside minimizes stale writes and memory overhead, whereas write-through guarantees cache warmness.
Pessimistic vs Optimistic Locking: Optimistic locking with versioning scales better under read-heavy traffic, while pessimistic locks prevent retry loops in high contention.

relatedAnswers.question: How do you handle high-concurrency contention when millions of users interact with RouteDefinition simultaneously?
relatedAnswers.interviewerIntent: Assessing candidate's deep knowledge of locking primitives, distributed concurrency, and database bottleneck prevention.
relatedAnswers.modelAnswer: To prevent write contention on RouteDefinition, we combine distributed caching with optimistic concurrency control (OCC). For reads, requests hit distributed Redis clusters with 99%+ cache hit rates. For writes, we utilize Redis Lua scripts or atomic CAS operations, with version-based optimistic locking at the database layer (UPDATE RouteDefinition SET status = :status, version = version + 1 WHERE id = :id AND version = :version). If high contention creates write hot-spots, we introduce queue buffering with Kafka partition keys to serialize updates per entity ID.
keyPoints: Optimistic locking using monotonically increasing version fields
Redis distributed locks with fencing tokens for cross-node coordination
Kafka topic partitioning by entity ID to serialize hot writes
Circuit breakers to fast-fail traffic during downstream latency spikes
relatedAnswers.tradeOffs: Pessimistic locking guarantees strict serializability but limits throughput and introduces deadlock risks. Optimistic locking maximizes throughput under moderate contention but requires client retry strategies during collisions.
relatedAnswers.edgeCases: Clock drift between servers when using timestamps instead of monotonic version numbers; network partitions causing split-brain master elections.

relatedAnswers.question: What is your data partitioning and sharding strategy for Design an API Gateway with Dynamic Routing & Rate Limiting (Kong/Envoy) as data grows beyond single-node limits?
relatedAnswers.interviewerIntent: Evaluating horizontal scaling competence, sharding key selection, and avoidance of hotspot partitions.
relatedAnswers.modelAnswer: We employ consistent hashing across database shards using MurmurHash3 on the entity ID. This ensures uniform data distribution across nodes. We configure virtual nodes (e.g. 256 vnodes per physical node) to avoid partition skew. For cross-entity queries, we maintain secondary global indexes asynchronously updated via Change Data Capture (CDC) pipelines like Debezium into Elasticsearch.
keyPoints: Consistent hashing ring with 256 virtual nodes per physical machine
MurmurHash3 / CityHash for uniform 64-bit key distribution
Asynchronous CDC secondary indexing via Debezium and Elasticsearch
Zero-downtime shard rebalancing with dual-write migration protocols
relatedAnswers.tradeOffs: Hash sharding provides uniform distribution but makes range queries expensive (requiring scatter-gather across all shards). Range-based sharding supports efficient range scans but creates hot shards on recent data.
relatedAnswers.edgeCases: Celebrity entities / hot keys overwhelming a single shard; handling network partitions during shard migration.

tradeOffs: Consistency vs Availability (CAP Theorem): Choosing AP for high availability with eventual consistency vs CP for strict serializability.
Cache-Aside vs Write-Through: Cache-aside minimizes stale writes and memory overhead, whereas write-through guarantees cache warmness.
Pessimistic vs Optimistic Locking: Optimistic locking with versioning scales better under read-heavy traffic, while pessimistic locks prevent retry loops in high contention.

relatedAnswers.question: How do you handle high-concurrency contention when millions of users interact with AgvRobot simultaneously?
relatedAnswers.interviewerIntent: Assessing candidate's deep knowledge of locking primitives, distributed concurrency, and database bottleneck prevention.
relatedAnswers.modelAnswer: To prevent write contention on AgvRobot, we combine distributed caching with optimistic concurrency control (OCC). For reads, requests hit distributed Redis clusters with 99%+ cache hit rates. For writes, we utilize Redis Lua scripts or atomic CAS operations, with version-based optimistic locking at the database layer (UPDATE AgvRobot SET status = :status, version = version + 1 WHERE id = :id AND version = :version). If high contention creates write hot-spots, we introduce queue buffering with Kafka partition keys to serialize updates per entity ID.
keyPoints: Optimistic locking using monotonically increasing version fields
Redis distributed locks with fencing tokens for cross-node coordination
Kafka topic partitioning by entity ID to serialize hot writes
Circuit breakers to fast-fail traffic during downstream latency spikes
relatedAnswers.tradeOffs: Pessimistic locking guarantees strict serializability but limits throughput and introduces deadlock risks. Optimistic locking maximizes throughput under moderate contention but requires client retry strategies during collisions.
relatedAnswers.edgeCases: Clock drift between servers when using timestamps instead of monotonic version numbers; network partitions causing split-brain master elections.

relatedAnswers.question: What is your data partitioning and sharding strategy for Design an Automated Warehouse AGV Robotics Navigation Grid as data grows beyond single-node limits?
relatedAnswers.interviewerIntent: Evaluating horizontal scaling competence, sharding key selection, and avoidance of hotspot partitions.
relatedAnswers.modelAnswer: We employ consistent hashing across database shards using MurmurHash3 on the entity ID. This ensures uniform data distribution across nodes. We configure virtual nodes (e.g. 256 vnodes per physical node) to avoid partition skew. For cross-entity queries, we maintain secondary global indexes asynchronously updated via Change Data Capture (CDC) pipelines like Debezium into Elasticsearch.
keyPoints: Consistent hashing ring with 256 virtual nodes per physical machine
MurmurHash3 / CityHash for uniform 64-bit key distribution
Asynchronous CDC secondary indexing via Debezium and Elasticsearch
Zero-downtime shard rebalancing with dual-write migration protocols
relatedAnswers.tradeOffs: Hash sharding provides uniform distribution but makes range queries expensive (requiring scatter-gather across all shards). Range-based sharding supports efficient range scans but creates hot shards on recent data.
relatedAnswers.edgeCases: Celebrity entities / hot keys overwhelming a single shard; handling network partitions during shard migration.

tradeOffs: Consistency vs Availability (CAP Theorem): Choosing AP for high availability with eventual consistency vs CP for strict serializability.
Cache-Aside vs Write-Through: Cache-aside minimizes stale writes and memory overhead, whereas write-through guarantees cache warmness.
Pessimistic vs Optimistic Locking: Optimistic locking with versioning scales better under read-heavy traffic, while pessimistic locks prevent retry loops in high contention.

relatedAnswers.interviewerIntent: Assessing candidate's deep knowledge of locking primitives, distributed concurrency, and database bottleneck prevention.
relatedAnswers.modelAnswer: To prevent write contention on TriviaQuestion, we combine distributed caching with optimistic concurrency control (OCC). relatedAnswers.question: How do you handle high-concurrency contention when millions of users interact with LruNode simultaneously?
relatedAnswers.interviewerIntent: Assessing candidate's deep knowledge of locking primitives, distributed concurrency, and database bottleneck prevention.
relatedAnswers.modelAnswer: To prevent write contention on LruNode, we combine distributed caching with optimistic concurrency control (OCC). For reads, requests hit distributed Redis clusters with 99%+ cache hit rates. For writes, we utilize Redis Lua scripts or atomic CAS operations, with version-based optimistic locking at the database layer (UPDATE LruNode SET status = :status, version = version + 1 WHERE id = :id AND version = :version). If high contention creates write hot-spots, we introduce queue buffering with Kafka partition keys to serialize updates per entity ID.

Kafka topic partitioning by entity ID to serialize hot writes
Circuit breakers to fast-fail traffic during downstream latency spikes
relatedAnswers.tradeOffs: Pessimistic locking guarantees strict serializability but limits throughput and introduces deadlock risks. Optimistic locking maximizes throughput under moderate contention but requires client retry strategies during collisions.
relatedAnswers.edgeCases: Clock drift between servers when using timestamps instead of monotonic version numbers; network partitions causing split-brain master elections.

relatedAnswers.question: What is your data partitioning and sharding strategy for Design a Thread-Safe In-Memory LRU Cache (Doubly Linked List + HashMap) as data grows beyond single-node limits?
relatedAnswers.interviewerIntent: Evaluating horizontal scaling competence, sharding key selection, and avoidance of hotspot partitions.
relatedAnswers.modelAnswer: We employ consistent hashing across database shards using MurmurHash3 on the entity ID. This ensures uniform data distribution across nodes. We configure virtual nodes (e.g. 256 vnodes per physical node) to avoid partition skew. For cross-entity queries, we maintain secondary global indexes asynchronously updated via Change Data Capture (CDC) pipelines like Debezium into Elasticsearch.
keyPoints: Consistent hashing ring with 256 virtual nodes per physical machine
MurmurHash3 / CityHash for uniform 64-bit key distribution
Asynchronous CDC secondary indexing via Debezium and Elasticsearch
Zero-downtime shard rebalancing with dual-write migration protocols
relatedAnswers.tradeOffs: Hash sharding provides uniform distribution but makes range queries expensive (requiring scatter-gather across all shards). Range-based sharding supports efficient range scans but creates hot shards on recent data.
relatedAnswers.edgeCases: Celebrity entities / hot keys overwhelming a single shard; handling network partitions during shard migration.

tradeOffs: Consistency vs Availability (CAP Theorem): Choosing AP for high availability with eventual consistency vs CP for strict serializability.
Cache-Aside vs Write-Through: Cache-aside minimizes stale writes and memory overhead, whereas write-through guarantees cache warmness.
Pessimistic vs Optimistic Locking: Optimistic locking with versioning scales better under read-heavy traffic, while pessimistic locks prevent retry loops in high contention.
